options: The top-level organizational unit inside a storage account — every blob belongs to exactly one
A virtual machine that runs Docker workloads
A synonym for a storage account itself
A type of Azure Function
questions.explain: Containers sit directly under the storage account and are the first segment of every blob path.

questions.q: What does a directory add, once hierarchical namespace is enabled?
options: Real, nested folder objects inside a container, as many levels deep as needed
A second storage account automatically
A brand new container with the same name
Nothing — directories exist even without hierarchical namespace
questions.explain: Without hierarchical namespace, there's no real directory object — just naming conventions, as Lesson 2 covered.

options: The container — the fixed first segment of the path
A directory that can be freely renamed
The file name
A storage account name
questions.explain: The container is always the first segment; everything after it is directory structure.

questions.q: Why do most real data lakes do the bulk of their organizational work with directories rather than containers?
options: Directories are free to create, rename, and restructure, while containers are a heavier, more fixed unit of organization
Containers cannot hold any data at all
Directories are more expensive than containers
Azure limits every storage account to exactly one directory
questions.explain: This is exactly why Lesson 10's data lake design and Lesson 11's zone structure lean on directories, not multiple containers.

questions.q: Where in the Azure Portal are containers created and managed?
options: The Containers blade under a storage account's Data storage section
The Azure Active Directory admin center
The Cost Management + Billing blade
A separate Containers resource type unrelated to storage accounts
questions.explain: Containers are managed directly from the storage account's own Containers blade, as shown in this lesson's screenshot.
